newsitem.title: IRAQ: Saddam orders armed forces to resist U.S. attacks.
newsitem.headline: Saddam orders armed forces to resist U.S. attacks.

text.p: Unbowed by U.S. missile attacks which he said caused little damage, President Saddam Hussein ordered his armed forces on Tuesday to down any hostile plane over Iraq and to ignore the Western-imposed northern and southern "no-fly" zones.

Saddam, wearing his field marshal's uniform, addressed the nation in a live speech on state radio and television just hours after U.S. air and naval forces fired 27 missiles at what they said were military targets in southern Iraq in response to Iraqi attacks on Kurdish rebels in the north.
"You men of the air defence and falcons of the skies consider from now their damned imaginary lines north of the 36th Parallel and south of the 32nd Parallel non-existent.

"Hit back with capability and efficiency, relying on God, the Almighty, at any hostile plane the aggressors fly to violate the airspace of your great country throughout Iraq from now and in future," Saddam said.
The United States and its allies set a "no-fly" zone north of the 36th parallel shortly after the end of the 1991 Gulf War to protect the Kurdish minority from further attacks by Baghdad's forces.
The "no-fly" zone south of the 32nd parallel was declared in the summer of 1992 to protect anti-government Shi'ite Arabs there.
Allied planes police the air exclusion zones from bases in Turkey and the Middle East, as well as from aircraft carriers.

Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz, in a telephone interview broadcast live on CNN television, said: "Iraq will not tolerate this 'no-fly zone' any more. It has gone beyond reason...(it) has been used as one of the means for aggression against Iraq."
Saddam said God "humiliated the aggression and the aggressors", stressing that Iraqi losses were minimal.
A spokesman for Iraq's general command of the armed forces, quoted by state television, later said the U.S. missile attacks had killed five people and wounded 19, including civilians.
"The sons of Iraq were on their guard for the aggressors, downing a great number of their missiles," Saddam said. He did not say how many U.S. cruise missiles were shot down.

"Once again the humiliated and lowly Americans have come to perpetrate their often-repeated cowardly act by hiding behind technological development God Almighty has turned into an insult on them and the opening for disgrace and shame that is to befall them," Saddam said.
"Resist them and teach them a new lesson in the meanings which their humiliating and lowly souls do not carry," Saddam urged his troops.
Aziz told CNN Iraqi military units who had helped a Kurdish faction regain the city of Arbil from a rival group had returned to their bases several hours before Washington fired missiles at Iraq.
"What we did was legitimate. What the United States did was illegitimate and against international law, against the letter and spirit of United Nations resolutions about Iraq," Aziz said.
"What we did was a responsible, positive, limited operation to help our people. We did nothing wrong."
Aziz dismissed official U.S. reports that Iraqi troops were still in Arbil or moving towards the Kurdish town of Sulaimaniya as "deliberate disinformation".
The official Iraqi News Agency (INA) quoted Aziz as saying Baghdad would complete the withdrawal of its troops from the Kurdish north on Tuesday.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said on Monday there was evidence that some of the Iraqi forces were penetrating deeper into Kurdish-populated areas and were threatening Sulaimaniya. The city, close to the Iranian border, is the last major stronghold of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) led by Jalal Talabani.

Repeating Iraqi charges that Iranian troops were helping PUK, Aziz said the Iraqi army only provided logistical support for the Kurdistan Democratic Party in the attack on Arbil and its operation was designed to thwart "the adventurism of Iran and the adventurist policies of Mr Talabani".
